analysis.title: AI Adoption in Focus: How Are Companies Quantifying the Benefits and Costs?
key_insights: MS used an LLM to analyze ~18,000 earnings, conference and investor day transcripts. On a trailing 12 month basis, 44% of S&P 500 companies cited at least one quantifiable AI benefit, up from 32% a year ago.
On a market cap weighted basis, 54% of S&P 500 market cap cites a quantifiable AI benefit, roughly flat vs 53% a year ago. The largest companies are furthest along in measuring AI impact.
49% of MS-identified AI Adopters now cite quantifiable benefits, up from 40%, though broadly flat since mid-year.

Productivity gain is the most cited benefit at 32% of companies (from 25%). Financial impact rose to 26% (from 16%), the largest increase of any category at 10pp, narrowing the gap with productivity from 9pp to 6pp.

Cost discussion is growing faster than benefit discussion: ~22% of S&P 500 companies cited an AI cost, up from ~8%. Among Adopters it was ~31% (from ~17%). On a market cap weighted basis ~42% cited costs (from ~33%).
~19% of S&P 500 companies cited both a cost and a quantifiable benefit, up from ~6%. ~85% of cost-citing companies also cite a benefit, but only ~43% of benefit-citing companies mention costs.

Token, inference and API costs are now the most cited cost category (12% of companies, from 1%), overtaking compute and infrastructure (6%, from 3%). MS reads this as lower unit costs accompanied by broader model usage, keeping total AI spend in focus.
Analyst questions often trigger cost discussion: 40% of S&P 500 companies have received analyst questions on AI adoption costs.
Financials lead on quantification: 67% of Financials cited AI benefits (from 42%) and 46% cited AI costs (from 14%). AI mentions per Financials company grew 80% Y/Y, the highest of any sector.
Communication Services (61%) and Information Technology (51%) follow Financials on quantified benefits. Materials was the only sector to decline (25% to 21%).
Companies in the top ~10% most frequently discussing quantifiable benefits show NTM EPS rising faster than the S&P 500 on a sector neutral basis.

MS says it has been writing about AI cycle broadening and sees further to go for the trade. It lists 'AI Adoption Leaders' screened on 3+ quarters of quantified benefits, AI Adopter classification, at least 10% upside to MS price target, and an OW or EW rating.
22% of S&P 500 companies cited a direct AI impact on their own labor, up from 14%. The market cap weighted share fell to 18% from 27%, so the broadening is driven by mid and small caps.

Labor themes are level: lower headcount growth/hiring and revenue-headcount decoupling at 11% each, AI automation of workers at 10%. Decoupling more than doubled from 5%. Layoffs tied to funding AI rose to ~3% from ~1%.
Financials (49%, from 33%), Tech (41%, from 35%) and Industrials (35%, from 21%) lead AI labor-impact discussion.

Reported AI-linked job cuts: AmEx ~3,500 (Oct 23, 2026), Barclays ~5,000 (Oct 2026), Microsoft voluntary buyouts expanded to ~60,000 (Oct 26, 2026), Kroger 3,000 corporate jobs, Block 4,000+, Meta ~8,000, Cloudflare 1,100+, Atlassian ~1,600, Coinbase ~700, Dow ~4,500.

Open-weights model use is broadening as a route to AI ROI. MS CIO survey: ~45% of companies use open-weights models, expected to roughly double to ~90% in three years. Open-weights are 8% of workloads today, expected 19% in three years.

Ramp data shows the top 1% of AI spenders (~$9K per employee per month) spend ~10x the top 10% (~$800), and the median enterprise spends ~$15. The top 10% spends about what the top 1% did three years ago.

If the pattern repeats, top-10% spend could rise ~10x in three years, partly offset by falling model prices and more efficient token use. MS says quantifiable benefits are necessary to broaden spend beyond top adopters.

MS 3Q26 CIO Survey: of CIOs able to assess ROI on token spend (n=58), 48% see ROI below token spend, 29% in line, 22% above. 43% of CIOs have AI spending controls, expected to reach ~75% by end of 2027.
Of respondents able to quantify the effect of spending controls (n=38), ~50% still expect token spend to grow and ~35% expect it to stay flat, so MS sees spend growing despite controls.

sector_views.rationale: Furthest along in AI quantification: 67% of companies cite benefits and 46% cite costs. Mentions per company grew 80% Y/Y. This is a data finding, not an explicit sector rating.
61% of companies quantify AI benefits, up from 47% off a small base.
Only sector where quantified AI benefit citations declined, to 21% from 25%.

earnings_insights: Companies that most frequently discuss quantifiable AI benefits show NTM consensus EPS rising faster than the S&P 500 on a sector neutral basis (FactSet data, MS analysis). These are consensus estimates, not reported results.

Company quotes cited from calls: ServiceNow Q2 revenue growth 23% with flat headcount and ~$500M of AI efficiencies this year. Snowflake Q2 product revenue +37% Y/Y. Figma Q2 FCF $53M (14% margin), with inference spend the largest driver of the Y/Y variance. Wix expects Base44 non-GAAP gross margin ~60% in 2H, from near zero entering 2026.

Asana gross margin 87%, down ~120bps sequentially, with ~80bps from AI infrastructure and compute costs. Wix Q2 total non-GAAP gross margin 67%, down 3 points Y/Y on Base44 investment and AI compute costs. Applied Materials Global Services gross margin 35.6% (+180bps Y/Y).
risk_factors: Only a handful of companies directly compare AI costs and benefits or quantify net return on total AI spend. ROI assessment remains early.
Rising token, inference and API costs as usage scales across workflows keep total AI spend in focus even as unit costs fall.
48% of CIOs able to assess ROI on token spend see ROI below spend, which could slow spending beyond the top adopters.
Top-10% spend could rise ~10x in three years only if quantifiable benefits broaden. Falling model prices and efficient token use could partly offset the increase.
Adoption remains bifurcated: median Ramp enterprise customer spends ~$15 per employee per month versus over $9K for the top 1%.

Market cap weighted share of companies citing AI labor impact fell to 18% from 27%, and market cap weighted benefit citations are flat (54% vs 53%), so broadening is concentrated in smaller companies.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 and 3 plot the share of companies quantifying AI benefits, 12M rolling: S&P 500 EW 32% to 44%, MC-weighted 53% to 54%, MS Adopters EW 40% to 49%, MC-weighted 64% to 55%.
Exhibit 4 plots the share quantifying AI costs: S&P 500 EW 8% to 22%, MC-weighted 33% to 42%, Adopters EW 17% to 31%, MC-weighted 49% to 56%.
Exhibit 32 projects Ramp AI spend per employee: top 1% at $9,568 per month and top 10% at $813, with scenarios for the top 10% following the top 1% trajectory or taking 10% and 20% haircuts.

tension_points.bull_case: Quantified benefits are rising (44% of S&P 500 from 32%), financial impact citations rose to 26% from 16%, and frequent benefit-discussers show faster NTM EPS growth. The top 10% of Ramp spenders could rise ~10x in three years if the top-1% trajectory repeats.
tension_points.bear_case: 48% of CIOs able to assess ROI see ROI below token spend. Cost mentions are rising faster than benefit mentions, only a handful of companies quantify net return, and spending controls are expected at ~75% of CIOs by end of 2027. Falling model prices and efficient token use could offset spend growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: MS says it will watch whether quantifiable AI benefits broaden over coming quarters to judge which way spend goes. Benefits staying confined to top adopters would undercut the broadening case.
